variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the Mercedes M279
variants.intro: The M279.980 engine code is stamped directly onto a machined pad on the engine block, typically located near the oil filter housing or the bell housing. It is also clearly listed on your vehicle's V5C registration document under "Engine Number" and can be decoded from the full VIN. **Common Confusion Warning:** Owners frequently confuse the M279 with other Mercedes flagship engines: - **M275**: The predecessor 5.5L/6.0L V12 biturbo. While mechanically similar, the M275 features different turbo plumbing, ECU mapping, and exhaust routing, making it incompatible as a direct swap. - **M177**: The newer 4.0L V8 biturbo. It features a completely different block architecture, hot-vee turbo sizing, and engine management system. - **M278**: The 4.6L/5.5L V8 biturbo. While sharing the hot-vee architecture, it differs significantly in displacement, cylinder count, and mounting. Fitting the wrong revision will result in severe ECU, wiring loom, and exhaust manifold incompatibilities.

relatives.description: The 5.5L/6.0L V12 biturbo it replaced; the M279 features twin-scroll turbos and direct injection, largely resolving the M275's early turbo actuator and thermal management weaknesses.
The V12 engine was discontinued after the 2020 model year in favor of electrified V8 and inline-6 powertrains across the flagship lineup.

The 4.0L V8 biturbo counterpart of the same modular era; owners of V8-powered S-Class or G-Class models should look here, as the M177 shares the hot-vee architecture but differs significantly in displacement and mounting.

items.answer: A Mercedes M279 engine replacement typically costs between £8,000 and £14,000 for a reconditioned supply-only unit [ESTIMATED - using M177 as proxy].

items.question: What is the most common failure with the Mercedes M279 engine?
items.answer: The most documented failure patterns for the M279 are timing chain stretch/guide wear and turbocharger wastegate rattle or bearing wear.
bullets: Early warning signs include a metallic rattle on cold starts, camshaft correlation fault codes, or boost pressure faults.
If the chain jumps teeth or turbo bearing wear leads to oil ingestion, a full engine replacement is required to prevent catastrophic damage.

bullets: This includes the S-Class (W222), S-Class Coupe (C217), Maybach (X222), and G-Class (W463).
You should always verify your exact fitment via registration lookup before ordering parts, as these are highly specialized applications.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Mercedes M279 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes M279 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the well-documented timing chain and turbocharger failure risks.
bullets: Used units carry a high probability of inheriting the same latent wear unless accompanied by stamped proof of preventative maintenance and no oil consumption complaints.
A proper reconditioned M279 includes verified cylinder bore integrity, new timing chain components, refreshed valley pan seals, and tested twin turbochargers as standard.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the M279 and not the M275 or M177?
items.answer: The M279.980 engine code is stamped on the engine block near the oil filter housing and is listed on your V5C registration document.
bullets: It is commonly confused with the older M275 or the newer V8 M177.
Fitting an M275 or M177 will result in severe ECU, wiring loom, and exhaust manifold incompatibilities, making like-for-like replacement essential.
